extracted.intended_audience: early-18th-century literate coffee-house readers; polite society readers of The Spectator
extracted.subtask_description: An issue of an early 18th-century periodical combining essays, theatre criticism, poetry, and foreign news intended for coffee-house and polite-society readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: “the drama introduced by the dialogue of the first scene with uncommon, yet natural conversation.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dialogue should read and sound natural rather than artificial; natural conversation can effectively introduce and propel dramatic action and engage the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lively, spirited characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should be 'drawn with much spirit and wit' and parts (e.g., Fondlewife) should be 'a lively image' of their traits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray characters vividly with distinct traits and energy so they embody their social/psychological roles (reluctance, fondness, impotence, etc.); lively characterization increases dramatic and comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'easy writing' and clichéd tropes
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism of 'easy writers' who produce 'sonnets on Phillis and Chloris, and fantastical descriptions'—a charge of facile, hackneyed verse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject facile, conventional poetic formulas and commonplace pastoral clichés; strive for originality and substantive craft rather than stock conceits that invite ridicule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verisimilitude / exact depiction of everyday life
rubrics_metrics.description: Praise for writing that 'described things exactly as they really appear' and 'makes the incidents just as they really appear' (example: a town 'Description of the Morning').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use precise, realistic details of ordinary life (street scenes, trades, sounds) to create lively, believable pictures rather than invented pastoral scenes where they do not belong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality / resist imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Warning that imitation of an original (e.g., the cousin's style) will be 'very insipid' and a refusal 'to admit of counterfeits.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage novel treatments and discourage slavish imitation; originality prevents works from becoming bland and derivative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatre as a moral and civilizing instrument
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendation of 'the apt use of a theatre, as the most agreeable and easy method of making a polite and moral gentry.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theatre can be used deliberately to form manners and morals in society; staging exemplary conduct and generous acts can move spectators and promote civility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power of performance to render poetic/historical character
rubrics_metrics.description: If painter and historian can move us, 'what may not be performed by an excellent poet, when the character he draws is presented by the person, the manner, the look, and the motion, of an accomplished player?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that actors' physical presence—manner, look, motion—amplifies written description; effective staging and performance can convey the full life of a character beyond words alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pastoral/dialogue that reveals human weaknesses with true raillery
rubrics_metrics.description: Praise for a pastoral dialogue (Sylvia and Dorinda) 'where all our little weaknesses are laid open... with truer raillery than ever man yet hit upon.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using pastoral or dialogic forms, aim to expose foibles and social weaknesses with truthful, incisive wit rather than flattening them into sentiment or cliché.
